summary.title: Best Practices for Designing a Pragmatic RESTful API
summary.one_liner: A practical checklist for designing a public REST API, covering resource URLs, SSL, versioning, filtering and sorting, field selection, pagination, envelopes, and JSON conventions.
keywords: http methods get post put patch delete
full text search api q parameter
json request bodies vs url encoded
takeaways: Treat an API as a user interface for developers: use plural noun resources with standard HTTP methods such as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE.
Version the API in the URL rather than in headers so resources stay browser-explorable, and always use SSL, returning a hard error rather than redirecting non-SSL calls.
Use query parameters for filtering (?state=open), sorting (?sort=-priority,created_at), search (q), and field selection (fields=...) to keep base URLs lean.
Return the created or updated representation from POST, PUT and PATCH, use 201 with a Location header on creation, and avoid response envelopes unless needed for JSONP or limited clients.
HATEOAS is judged not yet practical; the author recommends including resource identifiers and relying on documentation instead.
summary.summary: The author, writing while designing the public API for Enchant (a Zendesk alternative), lays out pragmatic answers to common API design questions. The post is organized as a series of sections, each giving a recommendation and its reasoning, such as RESTful URL mapping, SSL-only access, documentation, URL-based versioning (citing Stripe's approach), query-based filtering and sorting, and returning representations from write requests. It also discusses trade-offs for JSON-only responses, camelCase versus snake_case (citing a 2010 eye-tracking study), pretty printing and gzip (with a GitHub example measuring sizes), envelopes, and JSON request bodies. The page is an opinionated article rather than a standard, and it ends partway through the JSON request body section.
